Romanow: The Harrington School is pleased to come together to support Film/Media’s proposal to become a department at URI in the College of Arts & Sciences.
As a department, Film/Media (FLM) will be strengthened which will emphasize its crucial importance to our majors in the Harrington School of Communication and Media.
This action implements the clear priorities of the Academic Strategic Plans of both URI and Harrington, and places focus on the importance of Film/Media as we prepare our students to become future global leaders, offering them the necessary tools and technologies that will shape their professional careers.
FLM remains one of the unique interdisciplinary majors (and minors) at URI, with courses that count towards the major spanning 14 different disciplines across the University.

Departmental status will underscore and enhance the Harrington School’s national and global reputation, while placing FLM in a more competitive position so that our faculty can attract internal and external funding and grant opportunities, as well as encouraging internship and experiential opportunities for our students, and career advancement for our growing number of alumni.
Film/Media, serving 224 majors this Fall, although the second largest organizational unit in the Harrington School, is not given parity with the other units, which presents an unclear, confusing, and lopsided picture of the emphasis, resource allocation, and focus of the Harrington School and its aims, goals and the importance of its students within the overall structure.
This inequity sends a message to prospective and current students and their families that Film/Media may be less important and less vital than the rest of the Harrington School, and that it might not be the recipient of the attention and resources that a future major might desire.

Departmental status will situate FLM in a stronger competitive position to attract prospective students to the Harrington School and the future success and commitment to communications and media that the School promises.
FLM has long been a discipline that attracts potential University applicants, and it is necessary that we present a quality, fully formed department that enhances the entire Harrington School project and URI.
Film/Media is a central and vital discipline to the Harington School, the College of Arts and Sciences, and the University in assuring their goals, and this field surely requires its own department.

DEPARTMENT OF THEATRE Fine Arts Center, 105 Upper College Road, Suite 3, Kingston, RI 02881 USA p: 401.874.5921 f: 401.874-5618 web.uri.edu/theatre August 13, 2021 Dear President Parlange, Provost DeHayes, and Dean Riley, Please consider this letter to represent my support for the proposal by Dr.
Romanow and the Film program to achieve departmental status within the Harrington School.
It is my belief that a more developed Film department can only strengthen the university and, in turn, the Theatre department.
Film and Theatre both share similar developmental principals, organizational needs for production, and a sense of story telling through collaboration of artists.
The development of the Film program to a full fledged department will give students in both departments the advantage of a stronger working knowledge of the fields upon graduation.
Film and Theatre have been inextricably linked for a hundred years: both converging and connecting as methods and tastes change.
However, the two fields will be forever associated with the structural forms that create art: the process of planning, developing characters, and understanding the visuals that inform the piece.

Though a great deal of the Film program’s current emphasis is on the technical and pedagogical aspects of the field, I see, with a deepening of programming, an expanded body of artistic course work between Film and Theatre.
With careful planning as to not overburden either of our departments, I can envision a number of courses and work that could be developed within the two fields: Script Analysis and Script Writing, Acting, Directing, and Design.
Not only will the Film Department be able to develop their artistic course work, but I can see benefits for students within the Theatre BFA program, as they have more access to opportunities in recorded media.
We speak of preparing our students for opportunities.
A more robust Film department will support our students with more opportunities in the Entertainment Industry.
Though the Theatre department has integrated techniques required for recorded media in our curriculum, a stronger departmental presence of Film may lead to course work that develops a fuller scope for all students upon graduation.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Program is requesting that undergraduate students be able to declare a minor on Interdisciplinary Neuroscience by completing a minimum of 18 credits from the major.
Students must complete an application for the minor that is approved and signed by the INP coordinator and the INP Director.
Application for the INP minor must be filed in the INP Director’s office no later than the beginning of the student’s final semester or term but may be submitted as early as the first semester of the junior year.
Filing for a minor earlier than the junior year is subject to approval by the student’s degree-granting college.
A minimum grade point average of 2.00 must be earned in the minor courses, and a minimum of 12 of the 18 credits must be at the 200 level or above.
At least eight of the credits required for the minor must be earned at the University of Rhode Island.
Courses used to fulfill general education requirements may also be used for the minor.

Up to two courses required in a major program may be used to apply to both the major and minor fields of study (i.e., students may not obtain a minor if their major is interdisciplinary neuroscience).
Students may not take courses required for the minor on a pass-fail basis.
The requirements for the minor must be completed prior to graduation.
Successful completion of the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Minor will be reflected on the student’s official transcript upon graduation.
Graduates who have earned an undergraduate degree with a minor from URI and who are then readmitted to the university to pursue an alternate major or degree, may apply for that purpose all credits earned in pursuit of the previous minor field of study.
The specific course requirements for the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Minor include the following: • NEU 101: Foundations of Neuroscience 3 credits • NEU 110: Neuroscience Seminar 1 credit • NEU 210: Neuroethics and Diversity 3 credits • NEU 230: Neuroscience Professional Development 1 credit • NEU 262: Neuroscience Research Methods 4 credits • NEU 301: Cellular & Molecular Neuroscience 3 credits • NEU 310: Developmental OR NEU 320: Clinical 3 credits
